author_claim.quote: We confirmed that open-sourced LLMs operate in the strong superposition regime and have loss scaling inversely with model dimension, and that the Chinchilla scaling laws are also consistent with this behavior.

superposition.quote: Superposition means that there are more than m rows in W with non-zero norms

feature.quote: Each element xi in x is interpreted as the activation of this sample at feature i

operationalization.measured: How autoencoder reconstruction loss scales with hidden width m under weight-decay-controlled degrees of superposition in a toy model, and, for open LLMs, the row norms and mean squared overlaps of language-model-head rows plus evaluation loss as a function of 1/m.

flags.text: In the LLM analysis a 'feature' is a vocabulary token and its representation is a row of the unembedding matrix, not a property computed and used inside the network. Superposition found this way concerns output-token embeddings, not features carried by hidden-layer neurons.
flags.quote: As a naive mapping, we treat tokens as atomic features, with data dimension n equal to the vocabulary size.

flags.text: The test for 'strong superposition' in LLMs is that every token row has non-zero norm and vocabulary exceeds width. A trained LM head must give every token a non-zero row to predict it, so this test cannot fail and does not show that the model learned to compress more internal features than it has dimensions.
flags.quote: From the non-zero minimum norms and the fact n ≫ m, we confirm LLMs are in strong superposition.

flags.text: What superposition explains here is how loss scales with width, not polysemantic neurons. The toy model's hidden layer is linear (h = W^T x), so it has no neurons whose polysemanticity could be measured, and no neuron-level analysis of LLMs is done.
flags.quote: Result 3: Superposition is an important mechanism behind LLM neural scaling laws

title: Polysemanticity or Polysemy? Lexical Identity Confounds Superposition Metrics
claim: A substantial part of what metrics call polysemanticity reflects neurons responding to a shared word form (lexical identity) rather than compressed unrelated concepts.
setup: 2×2 factorial (same/different word × same/different meaning) over 407 polysemous words in nine transformers from 110M to 70B; SAE analysis; lexical-subspace removal effects on WSD and knowledge editing.
key_result: Lexical-only overlap consistently exceeds semantic-only overlap; 18–36% of SAE features blend senses; the confound lives in ≤1% of dimensions and removing it improves WSD and edit selectivity (p = 0.002).
stance_rationale: The conclusion states a substantial portion of measured polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition, which directly targets 'primarily'. The authors also say genuine superposition exists and the confound must be separated out first, and the study is limited to polysemous words, so the evidence pass gives -1.

blind_pass.rationale: Across nine transformers (110M-70B), a 2x2 factorial design shows that sharing a word form produces more neuron overlap than sharing a meaning. The conclusion says 'a substantial portion of what current metrics call polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition' (Fig. 1: 'only a small remainder is genuine superposition'). The authors explicitly do not deny superposition, and the 57% confound ratio applies only to polysemous inputs (Limitations), so the result argues against 'primarily' without refuting superposition.

author_claim.quote: A substantial portion of what current metrics call polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition.

polysemanticity.quote: describes the phenomenon in which a neuron in a large language model is activated for multiple, seemingly unrelated concepts.

superposition.quote: when a model lacks the dimensions to represent all its learned concepts separately, it packs more variables into its activation space than it has neurons.

operationalization.measured: Pairwise overlap (cosine similarity, Jaccard of active-neuron sets) of MLP intermediate activations at a target word across a 2x2 same/different-word by same/different-sense design (SemCor, 407 polysemous words, nine models), plus per-neuron sense selectivity (Cohen's d) checked with probing, mean-ablation and SAE feature collision counts.
operationalization.unit: neuron (MLP), with SAE latents as a secondary check

flags.text: The paper's 'polysemantic' condition is one word form used in two senses (bank/bank). A neuron that fires for a word form whatever its sense is arguably monosemantic for that token, not a neuron responding to multiple unrelated concepts. So the result tests one confound (homonymy) inside polysemanticity measurements, not polysemanticity across unrelated inputs in general.
flags.quote: PS (same word, different sense) measures overlap from shared word form alone

flags.text: Superposition is never measured: there is no count of features against dimensions. Whatever overlap is left after the lexical component is removed gets labelled 'genuine superposition' by elimination, so the paper does not show how much of the residual polysemanticity superposition actually explains.
flags.quote: Only a small remainder is genuine superposition.

flags.text: The headline says a 'substantial portion' of polysemanticity is lexical identity. But the lexically adjusted score reclassifies only 6.5-10.4% of flagged GPT-2 neurons, and the 57% figure holds only for polysemous inputs. The scale of the effect on polysemanticity overall is smaller than the framing suggests.
flags.quote: A substantial portion of what current metrics call polysemanticity is lexical identity, not superposition.

title: Neural Networks Are Already Clean
claim: Polysemanticity in the canonical vision examples came from fixable architectural and tooling problems and from 'recursive generalization', not superposition; most neurons in modern LLMs are legible.
setup: Essay (not peer reviewed; companion paper pending). Re-examines InceptionV1's canonical polysemantic neurons and the Zoom In car-dog circuit, retrains InceptionV1-style ConvNeXts across a 300x size range including a layer crushed 48x, and runs agent-driven neuron audits on Qwen3 and MoE LLMs.
key_result: InceptionV1's last layer goes from almost no to 99-100% interpretable neurons with architectural fixes at the same size; shrinking layers broadens neurons rather than packing unrelated concepts; preliminary Qwen3-32B audit finds ~90% of neuron poles have one main job and ~2-4% not yet understood.
stance_rationale: The essay claims superposition was the wrong explanation for polysemanticity ('Superposition' section; 'Superposition of the Gaps'). But it defines superposition as a learning principle that packs unrelated things into a neuron, and says it 'basically [doesn't] think' the question's sense, more features than dimensions, is bad news ('A Note on Superposition'). Its strongest evidence is in vision models; the LLM numbers are preliminary.
caveats: Essay, not peer reviewed; companion paper with LLM details not yet released
Strongest evidence is from vision models; LLM audits are preliminary
Uses a different definition of superposition from the question's count definition
Legibility percentages depend on thresholds for 'one thing'

author_claim.quote: The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues.

superposition.quote: So we keep the word and say exactly what we mean: neurons learning unrelated things together because they rarely interfere.

polysemanticity.quote: the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand

feature.quote: “feature” can mean something we care about, something the neural network has learned as a building block, or some mixture of the two.
feature.location: Appendix: A Note on Features and Definitions

operationalization.measured: Agent- and author-written explanations of individual neurons (counted per activation pole) in vision models (InceptionV1 and retrained variants) and LLMs (GPT-2 XL, Qwen3-32B, larger MoE models), judged as one main job vs. related offshoots vs. unrelated jobs, backed by steering, ablation, attribution graphs and watching neurons over training.

flags.text: The essay rejects superposition only in the sense of 'arbitrary packing' of unrelated things. It explicitly sets aside the count definition and grants that composition gives more features than dimensions. Its verdict that superposition is the wrong explanation is therefore not a verdict on the working definition.
flags.quote: We mostly set aside the sense in Toy Models, more features than dimensions, and not because it’s wrong.
flags.location: Appendix: A Note on Features and Definitions

flags.text: The step from 'neuron has several jobs' to 'recursive generalization rather than superposition' depends on investigators judging, after the fact, whether the extra jobs are 'related'. With a loose relatedness criterion (e.g. predicting that 'boat' comes next), almost any mixture can be absorbed, and no inter-rater or held-out test of that judgment is reported.
flags.quote: When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing.

flags.text: The LLM results are called preliminary audits, with details deferred to a companion paper, and the essay says full audits at trillion-parameter scale have not begun. Yet it states that the approach has worked up to trillions of parameters.
flags.quote: So far it has worked in language models too, up to trillions of parameters.

flags.text: The strongest evidence against superposition (retraining with architecture changes, watching neurons grow, toy and hand-built packing experiments) comes from vision models. The LLM evidence is mostly neuron-audit percentages, so the confident conclusion is stated for image models, not LLM neurons.
flags.quote: We’re fairly confident the image models we studied don’t have superposition.
flags.location: Appendix: Does Scale Help or Hurt Superposition?
